source.title: Task Discovery: Finding the Tasks that Neural Networks Generalize on
source.authors: Andrei Atanov; Andrei Filatov; Teresa Yeo; Ajay Sohmshetty; Amir Zamir

record.file_problem: The supplied full text includes the main paper and appendices; some figures are represented as extracted graphics and do not expose precise plotted values in text.
record.tranche_reason: Measures agreement among independently trained networks as a generalization-related property and tests whether natural and random labels differ; also reports test accuracy on natural and random-like tasks. It uses a different measure from the versions’ ordinary train/test error comparisons.
record.gate_note: Rows record the paper’s own experiments: agreement scores on human-labelled, random-labelled, and discovered tasks; agreement-score changes across architectures, training sizes, randomness sources, test domains, and adversarial splits; and stated green-pixel-task accuracy and adversarial-split accuracy. Do not treat cited results from other papers as this study’s findings. Figure-only comparisons without readable numeric values are not reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The study primarily measures inter-run prediction agreement, which cannot establish held-out accuracy on the specified labels. Section 3.2 states that both human- and random-labelled tasks reach zero training error, but does not report their paired held-out accuracies. The separate natural-label accuracy and distribution-shift experiments do not establish V1's same-recipe coexistence comparison. No other listed version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors present task discovery as a way to find diverse high-agreement tasks reflecting model and data biases, and use them to construct damaging distribution shifts. Their formal result makes high agreement necessary for sufficiently high accuracy, but not sufficient for accuracy on specified test labels; high agreement guarantees high accuracy only for a suitable consensus labeling.
record.recipe_differences: The paper measures inter-run prediction agreement and selected task test accuracy; it does not directly compare train and test error after fitting random labels under the claim’s specified recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Agreement varies with architecture, number of training images, which stochasticity source changes, test data domain, and task type. Agreement on discovered tasks is architecture-dependent; human-labelled task agreement is more volatile across test domains.

fits_no_version.finding: Human-labelled tasks have higher agreement than random-labelled tasks across architectures, training sizes and stochasticity sources; agreement also varies across test domains.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inter-run prediction agreement distinguishes task types and depends on the learning setup and evaluation inputs.

fits_no_version.finding: A network attains 0.96 accuracy on a pixel-threshold task, retains nearly that accuracy when other pixels are randomized, and falls to 0.5 when the defining pixel is randomized.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Networks can learn an input-dependent rule that is difficult for humans to infer visually.

fits_no_version.finding: Adversarial partitions reduce CIFAR-10 accuracy from 0.78 to 0.41 and ImageNet accuracy from 0.59 to 0.29.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Automatically constructed train-test correlation shifts can substantially reduce natural-label accuracy without changing pixels or labels.

fits_no_version.finding: Random-network tasks and optimized discovered tasks can have high agreement.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: High inter-run agreement occurs on input-dependent labelings beyond human semantic tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Agreement remains high in most adversarial-split cases even when target-label accuracy is near 0.5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Consistent predictions across training runs need not be accurate against a specified test labeling.

record.problems: Agreement score is explicitly not a general predictor of accuracy on the specified task labels. Several architecture, training-size, stochasticity, and test-domain results are only visible in figures without recoverable numeric values in the supplied text. The natural-label accuracy comparisons include adversarial distribution splits and therefore do not test ordinary same-distribution generalization under the claim’s specified recipe.
record.rows_left_out: Figure-only plots are recorded where the text describes a directional result; detailed per-task or per-domain plotted values were not recoverable and are not reconstructed. The task-similarity comparison in Fig. 6 is not linked to a listed claim version and is not a row.

untested.parts: The paired same-architecture, same-recipe comparison of random-label training fit, chance random-label held-out accuracy, and above-chance natural-label held-out accuracy. Zero training error on both task types is stated, but the paired held-out accuracy comparison is not reported.
Convolutional versus fully connected test error and the contribution of local connectivity; architecture comparisons here use agreement.
Adaptive versus SGD held-out performance under comparable tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All corrected states concern the listed claim versions, not whether the paper's agreement or distribution-shift findings occurred. The explicit zero-training-error statement in Section 3.2 should be retained as evidence of fitting capacity, but cannot substitute for the missing paired held-out accuracy comparison.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test fitting fixed random labels to near-zero training error and then comparing same-recipe held-out accuracy on the named Inception, AlexNet, MLP, or ImageNet settings. Its random-label result is agreement score; its accuracy example concerns a constructed green-pixel task.
